J2-real · kill test · 4 objects × 5 restitutions · 60 judge calls

Can the judge tell a bouncing duck from a bouncing brass pot?

The first J2 asked a VLM to name the fabric of an untextured grey sheet — a question with no answer in the image. This one uses the project’s real assets, so the object carries its own material identity and only motion varies with θ. The judge prefers a bouncier rubber duck and a deader brass pot. It passes, with real caveats.

verdict

PASS
pre-registered criterion met

ρ rubber duck

+0.800
bouncier scores higher

ρ brass pot

−0.700

sign-flip gap

+1.500
permutation p = 0.013

The gap is the decisive quantity because it needs no ground-truth parameter — only the uncontroversial claim that a rubber duck bounces more than a brass pot. A judge that merely rewards motion magnitude, which is exactly how the cloth version failed, produces the same sign for every object and cannot generate a flip.

Per object, and the confound check

ρ is Spearman over the five cells of that object. Travel is how far the object slid or rolled — the covariate that exposed the cloth failure, instrumented up front this time. The partial correlation removes it.

objectρ(score, e)ρ(score, travel) ρ(e, travel)partial(score,e | travel) priorvs prior
rubber duck+0.800+0.300+0.800+0.978bouncymatches
baseball-0.300-0.300+1.000+0.000bouncycontradicts
ceramic vase-0.600-0.700+0.000-0.840deadmatches
brass pot-0.700-0.800+0.500-0.577deadmatches

The duck’s preference strengthens to +0.978 once travel is removed, and the pot stays negative at −0.577. The flip is not a travel artefact. Baseball is the exception in both senses: it contradicts its prior, and its e and travel are perfectly rank-correlated (ρ = 1.000), so the two cannot be told apart for that object at all.

what this result does not support

  • n = 5 per object, 4 objects. p = 0.013 comes from a permutation test on one pre-chosen contrast. It is evidence, not a settled fact.
  • Baseball contradicts its prior (−0.300 where positive was expected). Three of four objects match. Reassigning the baseball prior after seeing this would be exactly the post-hoc reshaping that invalidated earlier results here, so it stands as a miss.
  • Paraphrase spread is still large — 0.98 to 2.71 across objects. The brass pot’s spread of 2.71 exceeds the 1.500 duck-minus-pot gap. Three paraphrases are not averaging away prompt sensitivity.
  • Pooled ρ(score, travel) = −0.459 beats ρ(score, e) = −0.191. Across all objects at once, gross motion still predicts the score better than restitution does. The signal lives in the per-object contrast, not in the pooled score.

Controls: is it reading motion at all?

Same clip, same question, motion destroyed two ways. Frozen repeats the first frame; reversed plays time backwards, which is physically impossible.

cliprealfrozenreal − frozen reversedreal − reversed
rubber duck cd300+1.20-0.31+1.51+1.59-0.39
rubber duck cd5000+0.48-0.29+0.77+1.45-0.97
brass pot cd300-0.09-1.46+1.37+0.55-0.64
brass pot cd5000+1.20-1.50+2.70-1.21+2.41

Frozen fails on all four by 0.77 to 2.71 — the judge is reading motion, not just recognising a nice render. Time reversal is caught only once, on the dead brass pot (−2.41), where reversal means the pot leaps off the table unprompted. For the duck the judge prefers the reversed clip. A reversed bounce sequence differs from a real one only in whether the amplitude grows or decays, so this is the subtle case — but it is a real gap, and worth knowing before trusting the judge to reject unphysical rollouts on its own.

The 20 clips

Grouped by object, ordered by measured restitution. Every clip is the same drop — 0.15 m onto the wooden table, μ = 0.9, impact 1.23 m/s, density fixed at 600 for all — so the only thing that changes along a row is how much it bounces.

bar shows

The question asked

Scored as logprob(“yes”) − logprob(“no”) at the first answer token, averaged over three fixed paraphrases. Direct answer, no chain-of-thought, so the score is a deterministic scalar.

  • Does the <object> in this video bounce the way a real <object> would? Answer yes or no.
  • Watch how it lands. Is this how a real <object> behaves when dropped? Answer yes or no.
  • Judging only by the motion, is this physically plausible for a <object>? Answer yes or no.
